newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mood upbeat on eve of inauguration.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mood upbeat on eve of inauguration.

text.p: On the eve of President Bill Clinton's inauguration for a second term, 60 percent of Americans approve of the job he is doing and 66 percent are optimistic about the next four years, a new poll shows.
A telephone poll of 1,307 people by CBS News and the New York Times Jan. 14-17 showed Americans feeling as optimistic as they have at the time of every recent presidential inauguration.

Sixty-six percent of those surveyed said they expected Congress and the president to be able to work together, but most did not expect significant progress on campaign finance reform, funding Medicare or balancing the budget.
Eighty percent said they did not expect the federal budget to be in the black by 2002, although a majority predicted taxes would be higher four years from now.

Generally, Americans had a favourable assessment of the economy, with 70 percent rating its condition as fairly to very good. Twenty-four percent said the economy was getting better and 56 percent expected it to stay the same, while only 19 percent expected a worsening.
Fifty-six percent of the people polled approved of the way Clinton was handling the economy, and the same percentage gave him a favourable rating for his leadership on foreign policy.
Only one in three thinks there will be another recession before the year 2000, the pollsters said.

The goodwill toward the president also extended to Hillary Rodham Clinton. For the first time in a year, significantly more Americans had a favourable impression of Mrs. Clinton than an unfavourable one. Sixty-five percent of those polled said they approved of the way she was handling her job as first lady.

Forty-five percent gave Congress a favourable approval rating, but House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, facing a reprimand and a $300,000 fine for ethics violations, won approval by only 32 percent of those surveyed.
Seventy-two percent said they did not believe Gingrich had more honesty and integrity than most people in public life, and 31 percent said they believed he had less.

The House ethics committee voted 7-1 last Friday to recommend Gingrich be reprimanded and pay a $300,000 penalty for using funds from tax-exempt organisations to pay for a televised partisan government course he taught and then giving the panel inaccurate information about what he did.

Thirty percent said they believed Clinton, facing numerous investigations into his own business, political and private affairs, had more integrity and honesty than most people in public life and 44 percent believed his was about the same as others, while 20 percent said he had less integrity.
The poll had a margin of error of three percentage points.
